title: I Enforced the Recording-Studio Overtime Minute on the Producer Who Invented It

parts.text: I booked until 9:00 p.m. and at 9:07 the producer started billing my card the overtime minute he had written into the rate card. He was still telling a story, not recording. The rate card said: OVERTIME BEGINS WHEN TRACKING CONTINUES. TALK IS WRAP. I was thirty-two, indie session, holding a 9:00 lock. Producer Ellis said, "Stories are tracking." I pointed at the card. He smiled. "Producers are the clock." I photographed the 9:07 talk, the card, and the silent DAW. Then I asked the studio manager to pull the session log. At 9:11 the manager asked why Ellis's name was on a talk-overtime ticket.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The manager can see a silent DAW at 9:07 billed as tracking against Ellis's own card.

social.video_title: He billed overtime for a story, not a take — Part 1/2
social.description: 9:00 lock, a talking producer, and a rate card he wrote. I pulled the session log. Would you have paid the minute?

parts.text: Ellis called it vibe until the log showed no takes after 8:58. I printed the ticket, the card, and the photo. The overtime reversed. Ellis told the lounge the card was always about optics. Optics is a word producers use when a DAW is silent. Session policy now has a second line: STORIES ARE WRAP. I keep 9:00. Ellis talks on his own clock. The booth finally ends when the file does.

social.video_title: Stories are wrap, not overtime — Part 2/2
social.description: Talk-overtime ticket, a reversed minute, and a second line on the card. Was vibe ever tracking?
